prompt: Where does the Cloud Billing export write the bill?

choices.text: Into a CSV file e-mailed each month
choices.why: The export is a table that grows, not a file.

choices.text: Into a BigQuery dataset
choices.why: Right. Every line of the bill becomes rows there, and any question about cost becomes a query.

choices.text: Into the project's audit logs
choices.why: Audit logs record who did what, not what it cost.

choices.text: Into a Pub/Sub topic of the billing account
choices.why: That is where a budget can publish, lesson 12.

prompt: Which part of setting up the billing export can be written in Terraform?

choices.text: The export itself, with its own resource
choices.why: There is no Terraform resource or gcloud command for it.

choices.text: Both, in one resource
choices.why: The export is switched on in the console only.

choices.text: Neither; both are console-only
choices.why: The dataset is an ordinary resource.

choices.text: The dataset it writes into
choices.why: Right. Switching the export on is done in the console, by somebody with a billing role.

choices.text: A dataset id takes no hyphens
choices.why: Right. Letters, numbers and underscores, and the provider checked before asking anyone.

choices.text: The name was already taken in BigQuery
choices.why: The plan asked BigQuery nothing.

choices.text: The project planner-logs does not exist
choices.why: The error names the dataset id, not the project.

choices.text: The location is not supported
choices.why: The corrected file kept the same location and planned.

prompt: Why does the finance group get `roles/bigquery.dataViewer` on the dataset rather than on `planner-logs`?
hint: What else is in the project?

choices.text: Dataset roles are cheaper than project roles
choices.why: Roles cost nothing.

choices.text: BigQuery roles cannot be granted on a project
choices.why: They can; it would just reach too far.

choices.text: On the project it would open everything kept there
choices.why: Right. A grant goes on the smallest thing that does the job.

choices.text: The export needs the role on the dataset to write
choices.why: This grant is for people reading, not for the export.

prompt: The planner switches the export on in November 2026 and is asked in December for the cost of each team in August. What can the queries of this lesson answer?

choices.text: All of it, since the export copies the account's history
choices.why: The lesson says not to count on history before it was switched on.

choices.text: August's total, though not by team
choices.why: The rows for August are not in the dataset either way.

choices.text: Nothing: those rows were never written
choices.why: Right. The cheapest moment to switch it on is the day the billing account is opened.

choices.text: All of it, once the dataset's location is changed
choices.why: A location is set once, and has nothing to do with history.

prompt: In the name of the export's table, each hyphen of the billing account's id becomes ___.
Where do the numbers in the lab's month of billing rows come from?

choices.text: make_export.py invents them
choices.why: Right. What is real is the shape of the rows and what the queries do with them.

choices.text: DuckDB downloads them from Google
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson reaches Google.

choices.text: The emulator records them
choices.why: The emulator is Pub/Sub only, and it bills nothing.

choices.text: A public sample of the planner's real bill
choices.why: The planner is the course's invented company.

prompt: Why is there no `labels.team` column to group by?

choices.text: The export drops labels
choices.why: They are in the row, as a list.

choices.text: Labels are a struct read with a dot
choices.why: `project` and `sku` are structs; `labels` is an array of them.

choices.text: DuckDB cannot read nested columns
choices.why: It read `service.description` with a dot.

choices.text: Labels are a list per row
choices.why: Right. A row's list holds a `team` entry or none, and it is looked for inside the list.

prompt: The export's `cost` column is `FLOAT64`. What does the lesson do about it?

choices.text: Converts every row to integer cents first
choices.why: That is rounding row by row, which makes the error larger.

choices.text: Rounds totals at the end, never row by row
choices.why: Right. Rounding each row first would add to the fraction-of-a-cent error, not remove it.

choices.text: Nothing; floats are exact for money
choices.why: A sum of floating-point amounts can be a fraction of a cent off.

choices.text: Reads the invoice instead of the export
choices.why: The lesson queries the export.

prompt: How many rows did `make_export.py` write for October?
`month.sql` reported 469.05 dollars. Why is that not what the invoice charges?

choices.text: It sums cost and leaves credits out
choices.why: Right. Credits are a list of their own on each row, and `net.sql` subtracts them.

choices.text: It counts October 31 twice
choices.why: There are 31 days and seven lines each: 217 rows.

choices.text: It is in reais, not dollars
choices.why: Every row says `USD`.

choices.text: It includes tax that the invoice leaves out
choices.why: The rows carry no tax.

prompt: In `net.sql`'s answer, how many dollars of credits did Compute Engine receive? Give the amount as a positive number.
hint: The credits column, without its sign.

prompt: Why are a row's credits summed inside the row before being summed across rows?

choices.text: Credits are already totals for the month
choices.why: They are per row, like costs.

choices.text: BigQuery forbids summing a column twice
choices.why: No such rule; the list is the reason.

choices.text: Each row has its own list of credits
choices.why: Right. A small query over the row's list gives one number per row, and those numbers add up.

choices.text: It makes the query cheaper
choices.why: It reads the same bytes either way.

prompt: `forgotten.sql` found sixteen dollars of N2 cores in `planner-dev` with no label. Which machine was it?
hint: The standard export has no resource names.

choices.text: The one named in the SKU
choices.why: A SKU names what Google sells, not a customer's machine.

choices.text: The query cannot say
choices.why: Right. The detailed export or a look at planner-dev's instances would.

choices.text: The data team's Pub/Sub machine
choices.why: Pub/Sub is its own service, and that line carries `team=data`.

choices.text: A machine in planner-prod billed to dev
choices.why: The row's project is where the cost belongs.

prompt: A report run against the real export, with no `WHERE` clause, shows a total several times larger than this month's invoice. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: It left the credits out
choices.why: Credits are a share of one month, not several times it.

choices.text: BigQuery's floats inflated it
choices.why: Floating-point errors are fractions of a cent.

choices.text: The detailed export doubled each row
choices.why: The two exports are separate tables.

choices.text: It summed every month in the table
choices.why: Right. Filter on `invoice.month`; it also keeps the bytes read, and so the query's price, down.

prompt: Match each DuckDB spelling to its BigQuery one.
Put the steps from nothing to a query about last month's cost in order.
hint: The dataset comes before the export.
items: switch the export on in the console
wait while a month of rows arrives
query with a WHERE on invoice.month
trap: Switching the export on first is the slip: it writes into a dataset, which has to exist for it to name.

prompt: The planner's finance lead asks for the team totals of last month, net of credits, every month. Which query does that need that this lesson did not write?

choices.text: forgotten.sql with every label instead of none
choices.why: That would list labelled rows, still gross.

choices.text: month.sql run once per team
choices.why: month.sql has no team in it and leaves out credits.

choices.text: None; the console's cost table is enough
choices.why: The lesson's point is that the export answers what the table does not.

choices.text: teams.sql with net.sql's credits and a month filter
choices.why: Right. Group by the team label, add the per-row credits, and filter on `invoice.month`.
